title: Course Schedule
statement: There are numCourses courses labelled 0..numCourses-1 and a list of prerequisite pairs [a, b] meaning you must take b before a. Return true if it is possible to finish all courses.
realWorld: Exactly what a build system, package manager or database migration runner does before executing anything. The 'circular dependency' error you have seen from Maven, npm or Spring is this algorithm reporting a cycle.

examples.explanation: Each course requires the other, so neither can ever start.
0, then 1 and 2 in either order, then 3. A diamond is not a cycle — direction is what matters.

bruteForce.whySlow: Each course re-explores the graph from scratch with no memory carried across runs. A subgraph already proven acyclic is re-walked up to V times, and with 2000 courses that is 2000 full traversals to learn one boolean.

patternIdentification: Model it as a directed graph: courses are nodes, prerequisites are edges. 'Can all courses be finished' is exactly 'is this digraph acyclic'. That is the cycle-detection half of a topological sort — run Kahn's algorithm and check how many courses came out. Two standard answers exist: Kahn with indegrees, or DFS with three-colour marking.

optimized.idea: Kahn's algorithm. Repeatedly take a course with no unmet prerequisites, count it, and decrement the counter of every course that depended on it. If all numCourses come out, the graph is acyclic; anything that never reaches indegree zero is waiting on something that is itself waiting — a cycle. Note we never need the order itself, only the count.
code: public static boolean canFinish(int numCourses, int[][] prerequisites) {
for (int i = 0; i < numCourses; i++) dependents.add(new ArrayList<>());
if (indegree[i] == 0) ready.offer(i);   // seed with ALL roots
return taken == numCourses;   // anything left is stuck in a cycle
// DFS alternative: 0 = unvisited, 1 = on the current path, 2 = finished.
// Meeting a node marked 1 is a back edge, i.e. a cycle.
private static boolean hasCycle(int node, List<List<Integer>> adj, int[] colour) {
int[] indegree = new int[n];   Queue<Integer> ready = new ArrayDeque<>();
for (int[] p : prerequisites) indegree[p[0]]++;  // count prerequisites
for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) if (indegree[v] == 0) ready.offer(v);
int course = ready.poll();  taken++;         // owes nothing - take it
if (--indegree[next] > 0) continue;      // still waiting on others
return taken == n;                               // short means a cycle

commonMistakes: Getting the edge direction backwards. [a, b] means b must come first, so the edge is b -> a and it is indegree[a] that you increment.
Seeding the queue with a single indegree-zero course. The graph is often disconnected, and missing a root truncates the count.
Using a single visited set in the DFS version; you must distinguish 'on the current path' from 'already finished', or a diamond is misreported as a cycle.
Forgetting to clear the on-path mark when the recursive call returns, which invents cycles that do not exist.
Not handling an empty prerequisites list — every course is immediately ready, and the answer is true.
